Hi Archy,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading Axle's price-curve documentation and got interested in what happens when the price signal changes after part of the original battery schedule has already run. At that point you're not really optimizing from scratch anymore; you're replanning around the energy you've already used and what the user still needs.

That's close to the planning work I'm already doing, and lately I've been looking for ways to apply more of it to energy and other problems where better decisions have a real-world effect.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to compare replanning strategies as successive price curves arrive and see which ones still meet the user's energy needs, but I'd much rather work on whatever flexibility-planning problem would actually be useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if there might be something worth working on, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

Andrew

Hi Nic,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Agtonomy's multi-point turns and got interested in the cases right at the edge of what the machine can complete, where a small change in available space means the same plan no longer works.

That's pretty close to what I spend a lot of my time on now: finding the conditions that make a plan fail and then searching for a way out. I've also been wanting to use more of that work on physical systems where getting the planning right actually changes what the machine can get done.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to build simulated turning cases around those limits and test how the planner recovers as the available space changes, but if there’s another autonomy problem the team actually needs help with, I’d be happy to work on that instead.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

body:
Hi Matt,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Agtonomy's multi-point turns and got interested in the cases right at the edge of what the machine can complete, where a small change in available space means the same plan no longer works.

That's pretty close to what I spend a lot of my time on now: finding the conditions that make a plan fail and then searching for a way out. I've also been wanting to use more of that work on physical systems where getting the planning right actually changes what the machine can get done.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to build simulated turning cases around those limits and test how the planner recovers as the available space changes, but if there’s another autonomy problem the team actually needs help with, I’d be happy to work on that instead.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

Best,
Andrew

I was reading about Spoor's bird tracking around wind farms and got interested in the short gaps where a bird disappears from view. Depending on what happened during that gap, the same visible track could suggest quite different accounts of how close it came to a turbine.

My current work involves searching for small changes that remove a recovery option. I'd like to use more of that simulation work on environmental problems, and testing what can actually be inferred from an incomplete track felt like a useful connection.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to replay tracks with controlled visibility gaps and build repeatable cases where the inferred encounter changes, but I'd rather shape it around a tracking-evaluation question the team already needs answered.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

Hi Rebecca,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Glacier's sorting robots and got interested in the choice between a good pick now and a better sequence of picks just behind it. With material moving past the robot, the value of a choice depends partly on what it leaves time to recover next.

That connects quite naturally to the search and planning work I do in automation. I've also been looking for ways to apply it where the decisions have a tangible result, and recovering more useful material from a waste stream is an appealing version of that.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to build and compare pick-selection logic on recorded or simulated streams, looking at what each strategy recovers under the same conditions, though I'd rather start with the planning problem the team actually needs help with.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

Andrew

body:
Hi Will,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about TerraClear's rock maps and how they guide field travel. What interested me was the choice of which rocks to prioritize when there isn't time to cover the whole field: the shortest route and the route that removes the most troublesome rocks may be quite different.

I've worked on layout and planning problems where reducing travel only helps if the useful work still gets done. I'd like to apply more of that optimization work to agricultural systems, where the result is something an operator can actually use in the field.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to compare routes and removal priorities within an agreed operating window, using a small simulation to make the tradeoffs visible, but I'd be happy to shape the work around whichever planning question matters most to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

Hi Matthew,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about running scientific simulations with Coiled and got interested in what happens when a large run is interrupted after some of the work has finished. Restarting the computation is one thing; knowing which results are complete and which still need to be produced is another.

I run simulations as part of my planning work, so this feels close to the tools I'd like to spend more time building. Making a long experiment easier to resume and trust would be a useful way to apply the recovery side of what I do.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to build a simulation example with controlled interruptions and test that the final outputs contain everything expected without duplicates, but I'd rather work on whichever part of the scientific-computing workflow would actually help the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

Hi Marco,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about ToffeeX's physics-driven design work and got interested in designs that are close at one operating point but behave differently as the load changes. A small change in the load could reverse which design you'd choose even if the performance estimates only move a little.

That connects to the simulation and optimization work I already do, where I try to understand which assumptions change the preferred plan. I'd like to spend more time on that kind of computational work when it feeds into something that will actually be built.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to build a comparison around an agreed set of designs and loads, showing where the preferred design changes, but I'd rather shape it around a design-evaluation problem that would be useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

Hi Steve,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about ev.energy's charging and flexibility modelling and got interested in changes that affect several drivers at once. A charging plan might cope well with one person leaving early, but several people making the same change could leave a very different set of options.

That's close to the planning work I do now, where a few changed constraints can make a previously workable plan impossible. I've been looking for ways to apply more of that work to energy, especially where better scheduling helps without asking people to change what they need from the system.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. I could build simulated departure changes and compare how the charging plan recovers, turning the difficult cases into repeatable tests, but I'd rather work on whichever flexibility-modelling question would actually be useful to your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

body:
Hi Jeffery,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Flash Forest's drone planting and got interested in how a route changes when you account for the next battery change or seed-pod reload. Finishing the nearest patch first might look efficient locally while leaving a longer return trip or a less useful starting point for the next flight.

That connects to the layout and planning work I do in automation, where travel and the order of tasks affect how much work a system can finish. I'd like to use more of that work on environmental projects with a physical result, which is what drew me to the planting operation.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around the planning. One idea would be to build a route-and-reload simulation and compare coverage under the same battery and planting constraints, but I'd much rather start with whatever operational planning problem would help the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

Hi Jonathan,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Treefera's use of satellite and ground evidence and got interested in the cases where two observations suggest different things happened in the same area. The useful next step seems to depend on what would distinguish those explanations, rather than simply collecting another observation of the same kind.

That connects to the search side of my work, where I try to find which next action actually changes what we know or can do. I've been looking for ways to use more of that work on environmental data that supports real decisions.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to build a reproducible set of evidence disagreements and compare which additional observations resolve them against agreed reference cases, but I'd rather start with whichever evidence-evaluation problem would help your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

Hi Alessandro,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Chloris's biomass and change measurements and got interested in how uncertainty carries between observations. Two estimates can each look reasonable while the difference between them is still difficult to interpret as growth or loss.

That feels close to the model-evaluation side of my simulation work: understanding when uncertainty changes the conclusion, rather than just the number reported. I've been looking for ways to apply more of that work to environmental measurements people use to decide what to do.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to build an evaluation around a reference set and test when uncertainty changes the inferred direction or size of biomass change, but I'd rather work on whichever change-detection question would be useful to the science team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

Hi Logan,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Rugged's construction layout work and got interested in what happens when part of the floor becomes temporarily unavailable after marking has started. The robot still has useful work it could do, but changing the order may affect how it returns to the unfinished area later.

That's close to what I work on in automation: recovering a useful sequence after one action becomes impossible, while keeping track of what has already happened. I'd like to apply more of that work to physical systems operating around people and changing spaces.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project I could take on. One idea would be to compare layout sequences around temporary obstructions in simulation and see which finish the remaining work with less revisiting, but I'd rather shape it around a planning problem that would actually help your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Civ's use of RTK positioning for construction layout and got interested in what happens when a good position estimate briefly becomes unavailable. Waiting in place, moving to another part of the job and revisiting later seem like choices whose value depends on what is still left to mark.

That connects to the recovery planning I do now, where the question is how to continue useful work after one part of the original plan stops being possible. I'd like to do more of it on machines working in the physical world.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to build offline positioning-interruption cases and compare waiting, revisiting and replanning against agreed accuracy requirements, but I'd be happy to work on whichever navigation or recovery problem is actually useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

body:
Hi Alex,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Civ's use of RTK positioning for construction layout and got interested in what happens when a good position estimate briefly becomes unavailable. Waiting in place, moving to another part of the job and revisiting later seem like choices whose value depends on what is still left to mark.

That connects to the recovery planning I do now, where the question is how to continue useful work after one part of the original plan stops being possible. I'd like to do more of it on machines working in the physical world.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to build offline positioning-interruption cases and compare waiting, revisiting and replanning against agreed accuracy requirements, but I'd be happy to work on whichever navigation or recovery problem is actually useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

Hi Aaike,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about VSPARTICLE's experimental datasets and automated material discovery. The part that interested me was what happens after a result disagrees with the current model: repeating a nearby experiment could clarify what went wrong, while trying something elsewhere could move the search forward faster.

That feels close to the search and planning work I do in biotech automation, where the next action depends on what the previous one revealed. I'd like to spend more time on computational work that helps decide which physical experiment is worth doing next.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to compare experiment-selection strategies on an existing dataset under the same testing budget, using the unexpected results as the starting cases, but I'd rather shape it around whichever evaluation would be useful to your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

I was reading about Assaia's turnaround monitoring and got interested in events that happen before the system learns about them. That's close to the planning work I do in automation, where the useful plan depends on both the physical state and what the system currently knows. I'd like to apply more of that work to operations with real timing and coordination constraints.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to replay turnaround traces with delayed or missing updates and compare the effect on estimated completion times, but I'd rather start with whichever event or planning problem would actually help your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

old.queue_body:
Hi Pierre,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Neural Concept's engineering models and got interested in two designs that receive very similar predictions. The useful question seems to be whether another full simulation would change which design you'd choose, rather than whether it would simply make one prediction more precise.

That connects to the simulation and search work I already do, where I try to spend computation on the cases that could change the next decision. I'd like to apply more of that work to design tools with a direct connection to physical engineering.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to compare predicted and simulated rankings on an agreed design set and evaluate which extra solver runs are most informative, but I'd rather work on whichever model-validation or design-search question would help the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Augmentus generating robot motion from 3D scans and got interested in a small change to a part's pose after a path has been planned. Sometimes adjusting a short section may be enough; in other cases, that local repair could leave the robot with no workable continuation.

That distinction is close to the planning and recovery work I already do. I've been wanting to apply more of it to physical automation, where the useful answer is whether the machine can still finish the job from the state it's actually in.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to build offline cases around changed part poses and compare local path repair with replanning, keeping the difficult cases as repeatable tests, but I'd rather work on whichever planning problem would help the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

body:
Hi Roy,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Augmentus generating robot motion from 3D scans and got interested in a small change to a part's pose after a path has been planned. Sometimes adjusting a short section may be enough; in other cases, that local repair could leave the robot with no workable continuation.

That distinction is close to the planning and recovery work I already do. I've been wanting to apply more of it to physical automation, where the useful answer is whether the machine can still finish the job from the state it's actually in.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to build offline cases around changed part poses and compare local path repair with replanning, keeping the difficult cases as repeatable tests, but I'd rather work on whichever planning problem would help the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

Hi Nick,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Albert's materials R&D work and got interested in the gap between a promising formulation suggestion and an experiment a team can actually run. Once ingredient availability and testing constraints are included, the most informative next formulation may be different from the one that looks best in the model.

That feels close to the constrained planning I do in biotech automation, where the useful choice has to account for what the physical system can do. I'd like to apply more of that work to experimental decisions with a clear practical outcome.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to build an evaluation around an agreed formulation problem and compare selection strategies under its real constraints, but I'd rather work on whichever experiment-planning question would actually help the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

body:
Hi Xianchao,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Realtime's multi-robot planning and got interested in what happens when one robot is delayed after the paths have been planned. The paths can still be collision-free, while the order in which the robots can move through a shared area has changed.

That's close to the failure and recovery work I do now, where individually valid actions can leave a system with no useful way to continue. I'd like to apply more of that work to physical automation where finding a different sequence lets the machines finish the job.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to search an offline cell model for small timing changes that disrupt the sequence, then reduce them to cases the team can replay, but I'd rather shape the work around whichever planning problem would actually be useful.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

body:
Hi Achyut,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about FruitScope's repeated passes through an orchard and got interested in how you separate a change in the fruit from a change in what the cameras can see. The same trees can look quite different when fruit is hidden by the canopy on one pass and visible on the next.

That connects to the evaluation work I've done with models running on physical robots, where a change in the observation can affect the result. I'd like to use more of that work on agricultural systems that help people make decisions in the field.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to compare paired passes against an agreed reference and test which visibility changes alter the count, but I'd rather start with whichever perception or evaluation problem the team actually needs help with.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

body:
Hi Filip,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Gideon's trailer loading and got interested in placements that work for the current pallet but leave less room for the next move. Once some of the trailer is already loaded, finding a way to continue is a different problem from planning the whole sequence from scratch.

That's close to what I work on in biotech automation: finding the conditions that leave a system stuck and searching for a recovery from the state it's already in. I'd like to do more of that planning work on machines operating in physical spaces with changing constraints.

That made me want to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project. One idea would be to search simulated loading sequences for those cases and compare ways to continue with less undoing of completed work, but I'd rather shape it around whichever autonomy or recovery problem would help your team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew

body:
Hi Colin,

I'm a UofT student on co-op in London, UK, working on search, planning and simulation for biotech automation, mostly around failure and recovery in large systems. I've also done a fair bit with RL and MCTS.

I was reading about Carbon's laser weeding and got interested in cases where a weed is partly hidden by a crop. The part I wondered about was whether the model's confidence changes as the view gets less informative, or whether it can stay confident after losing the detail it was relying on.

I've worked on evaluating a vision-language-action model and getting it running on physical hardware, so understanding what a model can reliably infer is something I'd like to spend more time on. Agricultural robotics is particularly appealing because those predictions lead to a concrete action in the field.

I wanted to ask whether there might be room for a small contract project around that. One idea would be to build an offline evaluation on an agreed image set and compare confidence with the result as crop and weed overlap changes, but I'd rather work on whichever perception-evaluation question would be useful to the team.

Happy to hop on a call if it sounds worth exploring, and happy to send over my resume as well.

Best,
Andrew
